utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave, only two words before the witness is brought into the courtroom. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witness who will be called after this witness will be General Radovan Radinovic. The Prosecution has the expert opinion of General Radinovic, and I think that we disclosed it in November last year. We hope that the Prosecution has read the document because they had enough time to do that. But the Prosecution sent us, a few hours before General Radinovic's testimony, a fax of which they said that they were surprised that a large number of documents have not been -- had not been disclosed, referring to footnotes. This was done a few hours before we hear this witness, even if they had plenty of time to do that if they really wanted to do that. We think that there are certain things that can be done on occasions and others no. We think that if the Prosecution had wanted these documents, then they practically had a whole six months to do that. And we think also that the Defence does not have to disclose indirect references to a particular work - I'm referring to footnotes - and especially to respond to a request which happens a few minutes before such an important testimony. I do not think these are hard words, but I think that this -- such a request is not acceptable in our opinion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think the words are too hard, perhaps a bit too many in order to say what you had to say. Mr. Ierace, would you please respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. To say that there are some problems with the disclosure of documents in relation to General Radinovic would be an understatement. I can assure the Trial Chamber that we have not delayed in making this request to the Defence. There have been exhaustive searches done by staff of the Office of the Prosecution of the documents cited in the footnotes to Dr. Radinovic's report. And by this morning it was apparent that we were unable to match many of the documents. We did discover by experimentation that some of the references to the documents were incorrect and by doing searches of neighbouring numbers, we were able to discover some. This letter which I think you have a copy of, Mr. President, is the -- lists the documents that we were not able to locate. Rather than raise it in the first instance with the Trial Chamber, having regard to earlier requests by the Trial Chamber, we thought it appropriate to first give the Defence an opportunity to respond to see if they could find the documents. I can only agree with my learned colleague that this matter should not arise a matter of hours before such an important witness is called. I don't think it's the fault of the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The Chamber will consider the matter. If, however, there would be mistakes in the references, of course, that would make the job, I would say, both for the Defence and the Prosecution very difficult. Primarily the expert witness himself is responsible for the correctness of his citings. But if the parties can compare, especially those footnotes where there have been problems, I take it that both parties would have been confronted with it. We'll consider the matter, and we only got the letter five seconds ago. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, I merely wanted to say that I checked some of the footnotes before I came into the courtroom now, and I have told my colleagues that the footnotes 73 and on were all the documents that the Defence was referred by the Prosecution. These are the documents of some of the units. The only problem with this is that General Radinovic when he used them did not indicate ERN numbers, but it is a problem for us since these documents were not in chronological order. It is a problem for us now to find them. But he used them when he made references to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was exactly -- what did you say about these documents? Because that's not clear to me. Are there errors in the footnotes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are no ERN numbers, so it is difficult for us to find them quickly. And there are -- these are documents of the BH army which the Prosecution disclosed to the Defence but these documents are not put in chronological order, that is, by dates and by years, which would help us to find them quickly. But -- and there are only dates marked, and I told my learned friends that that was a problem because the general did not write address the document with ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand on the basis of this letter you started searching these documents in order to assist the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I also would like to seize this opportunity, since I am on my legs, and I hope you will allow me to do that. I wanted to inform you, but I believe you already know about General Galic's request with regard to a period between the 14th and the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that I'm aware of these dates specifically, but it might have been that I missed something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I was not in the building this morning, I missed that message. I do understand that it has been -- that it has been raised with the legal staff and the registry. The 14th and the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time between the 14th and 23rd, because the visit of General Galic's family has been approved. He hasn't seen his wife for quite some time and they have some family problems, so he's asking if during that period of time we could have a short break. It is all within the context that we already discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that we would have a short interval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I explained to the parties what the Chamber has in mind. That means after finishing the Defence case that we would have a break of a couple of days so that the Prosecution could immediately express itself, the Defence could then respond, and then we could start with any rebuttal evidence if we -- if it -- if there's any application to present rebuttal evidence. That would be a couple of days. The same would be true for the week when the rebuttal evidence has been presented so the Defence, for any evidence in rejoinder, can apply for leave to present any evidence in rejoinder. That would create a couple of days as well. Then finally, before we -- the parties will be allowed then - I think I did not yet mention that - will be allowed two weeks to prepare for their final briefs, and then we'll have the closing argument. When -- I think I did not tell this part of this schedule yet, but that's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what the Chamber has in mind to do. If it fits within these breaks, of course, there's no problem. But the Chamber would be very hesitant to introduce other breaks. So it partly also depends on the parties itself, how we proceed, whether this will be possible. But I have to look closer at the tentative schedule we have drafted until now so that we see whether this fits in in March, between the 14th and the 23rd. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very well. It is wonderful that you are telling us now about this week when we shall not work and for the following reasons. The first one, that we've answered the question that you asked us, Mr. President, concerning the necessary record about our request for the disqualification. Mr. President, we've talked to the registrar, but we believe that the file has to be presented to the Appeals Chamber. We have presented our direct observations to the Appeals Chamber, of course with a copy for your Chamber, of course. So this is the first question, because we still insist to request the suspension of this hearing. Secondly, we wish also to -- we have officially a document, a motion which seems to derive from a non-governmental organisation in the United States and which makes a reference to a number of -- to a very large number of decisions and situations, and we are -- want to ask, do you want us to answer that? What are we supposed to do? I do not know that. Secondly, for this type of intervention, are there any standards which would apply to the Defence, the number of pages that such an intervention, such a response could take? And it depends on your decision. And if now we ought to also to respond to numerous arguments which come from another part of the earth. We believe that all this would take a lot of time, but it depends on the length of the answer that we are allowed to provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In answer to what exactly, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? To the -- to the Martin document or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly. Yes. Francisco Forrest Martin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has received a document which applies for leave to be admitted as an amicus curiae because without leave you can't serve as an amicus curiae. In Rule 74, it reads that, "If the Chamber considers it desirable, that the Chamber can invite or grant leave to a state and organisation or a person to appear before it and make submissions on any issue specified by the Chamber." It seems that Mr. Martin attached already whatever he would like to submit to the Chamber on his request for leave. The Chamber has considered whether it would invite the parties to submit their views on whether Mr. Martin should be granted leave to appear as an amicus curiae. The Chamber has decided that it would not invite the parties but at the same time if the parties would like to submit their views on it, the Chamber will then receive whatever the parties would like to bring to the attention of the Chamber, and then we'll have to decide whether leave will be granted or not. So the first question is not, I would say, to respond to the full argument set out, but the first question would be whether leave should be granted or not. If leave will be granted, then of course we have the opinion, the legal opinion - it's more or less a legal opinion, I would say - on certain issues, and then of course the parties could respond but then more in -- to the content and not to the question of whether leave should be granted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the parties, however, would like to submit something, this application has been made in a very late stage of the proceedings. We would then like to receive your submissions, well, let's say, within a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Impossible practically. Do you think our position regarding the procedure, that is, whether such a leave should be done or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that if you read through this document, that the first question would be that -- whether it would be desirable for the proper determination of this case to have this opinion of the amicus curiae only if a positive answer would be there and if the Chamber would decide that it would grant leave, then of course the next matter would be that perhaps the parties would like to address the matters raised in the amicus curiae document. Yes? Then, Mr. Usher, if the Defence is ready to continue for another 15 minutes the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was 20, Mr. President, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it was 20 yesterday, it's 20 today, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- you're right. It's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Kuljic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. You'll now further be examined by counsel for the Defence. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we are going to have a look at, in particular in relation to terror, other ulterior confirmations that you have found on the Internet. First of all, the site of the national library of medicine, is that a professional, recognised site; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as this is stated on the site, and it is used as such. My colleagues use it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Doctor, with respect to the post-traumatic stress disorder that you said you knew professionally, this syndrome, what can you tell us about this in relation to Sarajevo and in relation to the articles that you have found, particularly with respect to percentages as to certain groups of population of military personnel and with respect to some groups of civilians?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that there are many articles that were published in a number of countries. People who dealt with refugees and people who assessed the post-traumatic stress disorder in refugees. What was very interesting for me was a recent publication by a group from Munich who did a residential sample, that is, in Sarajevo itself, they found that from the people who they questioned on the ground --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd be grateful whether it could be clarified, firstly whether this article in particular is one of which we have a photocopy. And if not, I have a further -- I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, Dr. Kuljic: The study you referred to, a publication by a group from Munich, is this in the documents you gave to us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document which I gave -- I can't quite remember, because I had loose copies, and I later on found this copy in my notebook. So it may have remained in the room, if it's not among the documents. What I mean, it's strange that I'm just talking about this, because I have a lot on my mind. It's quite hard for me to tell you everything, but I can later on forward these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is that the Prosecution should also be in a position to prepare for cross-examination. So therefore, all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sources should be known to them. But do you have a name? Because you say you're not quite sure whether it's in this material or not? You referred to a group of Munich and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually the source named, I don't see at this moment any Munich.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, but I don't know whether this was a mistake, but I believe that this is not in among the documents that we were given yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, is this a study by a certain gentleman called Rosner?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Here in some of my notes I can see that I have handwritten that I wanted to mention Rosner's study and to compare it with the other study.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just -- is Rosner mentioned anywhere in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, this is a new study which I found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there is no mention made of Rosner in the documents you gave to us yesterday. So then we are in a situation where Mr. Ierace wanted to raise an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my objection is that this evidence should not be permitted. It's a rather rhetorical question, but how am I to respond without having at least a copy of the publication and time to read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think that it is not always necessary to have a document, a written document before oneself, when we are speaking to an expert. To make an example, I can remember that I had a client who was a star of the dance, who was over 70 years old and was telling me, "this is very simple, I make movements with my hands and everyone understands." Now, this is a good example to use here. If the doctor knows certain things, if he knows figures, he can formulate them without us needing to read the text to know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't need the text to be read, but the Prosecution needs the text to prepare for cross-examination. That's the issue. Let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is partially sustained. No questions at this moment about this source and the subject covered by this specific study. The Defence is invited to provide a copy of the Rosner, if there's an excerpt, if there's a summary, to the Prosecution. And we always then can see, not knowing at this moment what the study is about and perhaps the Chamber could be provided with a copy as well so that we can see what the study is, whether it's a summary that could be read easily, whether it's something entirely new. We are not aware of that. And then the Chamber can always reconsider the position upon the request of the parties, either to allow the -- the Prosecution may --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the doctor has this document on him at this very moment in order to save time, can we propose that the usher can have a copy and make a copy so that we can have it as soon as possible and we'll know about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, what I have to say relates to that. The Prosecution -- I don't mind saying this in front of the witness. The Prosecution has made every attempt to obtain the articles referred to by the witness yesterday and the synopses of which are in the document provided to us. We're unable to get access. They're not obtainable through the Internet. We're told by the library it would take some seven days to get the articles. What we've been provided with are simply the synopses. And it may be that it's a synopsis that the witness is referring to in relation to the Munich study. I'm mindful of the Trial Chamber's interest in allowing in as much relevant material as possible, I wonder whether an appropriate course might be for us to obtain these articles. I'm happy as soon as I get them. If I can obtain them from other sources more quickly, and I may be able to, to circulate them, and the witness be re-called, perhaps during the evidence of General Radinovic, for further questioning. That's a way which would enable all of these issues to be ventilated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course there's -- I should then first ask one thing to you, Dr. Kuljic: The document you provided yesterday, these are synopses, these are abstracts. Have you read the originals or not? I mean, if you -- well, let's say the first page, the article of Jensen. Did you only read the abstract or did you also read the ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read the abstracts here because it's a large number of cases. But the point of the abstract is to give a very concise information. It is a digest and the essence of the abstract cannot differ from the essence of the actual document, of the paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, usually it's not, at least the purpose of an abstract is that it gives precise information. But I do understand you have not consulted any of the original articles underlying these abstracts. Is that a correct understanding, or did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These that I have attached yesterday, I hadn't read them in the original, no, not those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, both parties and the expert witness himself only have available at this moment as a source the abstract of the article. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That doesn't overcome the problem, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not entirely perhaps, not your problem. But of course we are now in a situation where at least all the parties have the same information and the expert has the same information as well. We'll consider whether it will be necessary to have all the underlying documents. But if they are found, of course, I expect the parties to disclose it to the other party. Whether this would be a reason for a re-call of a witness is something still to be considered, Mr. Ierace, and we'll consider that. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But I'd ask just one question to your Chamber: Could we give the original of the Rosner document to the usher so that it can be copied in the meantime? And you said yes but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although, it would have been really appropriate, having seen that it was not among the material distributed yesterday and since you had, it seems in mind, to -- you have the article, and you even did not have to consult your papers to refer to the name of Rosner. That means that you were perfectly aware that questions would be put in respect of this article, which was nowhere in the sources. So it would have been appropriate, first of all, to copy it prior to this hearing; and second, then do it yourself. But we'll now ask whether we can get the assistance of the usher. If you'll please proceed to -- --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... And we'll see whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the doctor would be good enough to hand the document over, the Rosner document, if you have it, Doctor? Do you have this extract from the Rosner article, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to check here. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yes, this is Rosner's article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if there would be a possibility perhaps with the assistance of the usher that it could be copied six, seven, eight times. It's just one page. Then please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. What can you tell us, still in relation to terror? Can you tell us about the indicators that could be given in this field, in terms of weight of children at birth, nutrition, good or poor, of mothers in Sarajevo this time, and the scientific studies that were recently produced about the subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. I'm not aware of any evidence so far to the effect that the weight of children at birth is an indicator of terror, so to that extent it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any evidence presented at this moment that ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. You authorised me to ask the questions about the articles that were found by the doctor in the reference that he gave us, which was an Internet reference, and I can see that we have this before us so I'm asking questions in relation to this. I can see an article which is entitled "Nutrition and -- [In English] Of women and children in Sarajevo during July 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that I'm putting questions to the witness in respect of documents he presented yesterday. That's what Mr. Ierace --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since we have had an opportunity to read the documents, that questions could be put to the witness in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have no difficulty with that, Mr. President. Simply that the -- the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's still leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yeah, there's no mention of terror in the article, and that's the connection that the learned counsel makes in his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So would you refrain from leading and put questions to the witness if --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to your report and also in relation to your experience, what can you tell us which would be of assistance for this Chamber or the Prosecution or the Defence about the problem that I mentioned, please?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this data that was mentioned is in relation to the report of Dr. Turner. In his report, he gives a statement of one of the witnesses who said that the population was going hungry, and I gave this data here and you can see that this is a report by the officials of the World Health Organization and they say that there was no famine. There is a number of articles. I said that these articles were all grouped in several groups, that they were all attached together. I'm sorry that during the photocopying these articles were scattered. So if they were all put together, it would have been easier to understand. This article about the nutrition of children, it is mentioned that there was no registration of a large number of children who were suffering malnutrition, that they were of very low birth weight, and that even children who were older, there was no percentage that was higher found in relation to any other group of population because we can see that 2.6 per cent of children who were suffering malnutrition, this is an article Dzumhur Zec Buljina, this was from the paediatrician's clinic in Sarajevo up to March 1994. And what is also mentioned here, this is Robertson, Fronczak article on nutrition saying that there was no data saying that there were children that were -- there were more than 2.5 per cent of children who were suffering from malnutrition. What's very interesting for me here as a psychiatrist is that also in this article what was found is that women in Sarajevo were not breastfeeding their children sufficiently, and because of that what was confirmed in further articles is that there was a promotion of breastfeeding following that, as this was pointed in Moro work about the Dobrinja hospital, as it says here, and it is well known that women under stress have a problem with breastfeeding. So because of a lap of dopamine and prolactine they suffer lack of breast milk, which is why children cannot be fed. What was so interesting for me is that in situations of extreme stress and war, as this is given in the Turner expert report, the population continues to have the same level of nutrition as well as children and women continue to breastfeed their children. So this is all in relation to the nutrition of children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Doctor, what can you tell us, what was the conclusion of this article in relation to the possibility for mothers, first of all in Dobrinja, to normally breastfeed their children?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here in Cemerlic-Zecevic paper in a conclusion by the end, I had underlined it, fortunately, so you can find it immediately. It says that "War and suspension of nutrition didn't produce any negative effects in the growing of children and occurrence of anemia. What can happen is that there could be more breastfeeding instances and also there would be additional food, additional nutrition that was given and also with additional good parental care. But I also have to stress that the prolactine hormone which influences breast milk, production of breast milk, because it is also influencing the brain, as well as the care for the children. .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now, the figures that you were able to find, in relation to the problem of suicide in Sarajevo, if we compare it to other republics in the former Yugoslavia, what can you tell us according to these articles?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'll tell you my train of thought. Why I came to that is because in Turner's report it is mentioned that in one of the statements of one of his witnesses what was said, that he had heard that there was talk in the hospital that there was an increased number of suicides. The comment of Dr. Turner's was that he did not find an increased number of suicides but that if we consider chronic stress during this period, this could be expected. So this was his expectation. Now, I can show you the findings by Jensen and the World Health Organisation was that they supposed that there would be an increased number of suicides throughout the time and there were other factors which are relevant for this debate, and there was an expectation there would be an increased number of suicides. Now, very frequently in medicine we find that there is some expectation which sometimes is not confirmed. In the work of Slodnjak from Ljubljana he compared a group of Bosnian refugees with Slovenian adolescents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness is jumping from source to source. We've heard a reference to Jensen and suicide rates, and now to someone else in relation to Bosnian refugees with Slovenian adolescents. I'd be grateful if we could have the source each time the witness refers to one in terms of whether it's an Internet abstract or -- whichever document it is which has been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please in such a way -- I take it that when you refer to Jensen, it might have been to one of the articles from the Internet you gave us yesterday. But could you please indicate as precise as possible so that both Prosecution and the Bench can follow in more detail what you tell us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could the witness be asked to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have to ask you on the request of the interpreters to slow down your speed of speaking. I tried already with my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hands once to ask your attention for that because you're speaking really very quickly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, please, could you please continue the moment when you were talking about an increased figure of suicides. Was that in Sarajevo or was it elsewhere? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To start with, I'd just like to say that the Prosecution probably failed to hear what the Presiding Judge said to speak just about the articles that are only here. So the articles are all here. But I don't mind continuing with this new observation. Now, one of the articles that I gave you yesterday, this is Jensen's article, "Mental health in war conditions." And I don't have to give you the entire title. And this article, I have also underlined the relevant parts, that it says here that, "Complications that are linked to war trauma and that are causing stress and problems to do with stress, and they can cause an increase in alcoholism, criminal behaviour, and suicide." Now, the point was suicide. After that, I mentioned the paper that was given yesterday. That was Slodnjak, "Depression and parasuicide in -- depression in Slovenia." I hope that you were able to find it. They were put one after the other. I've also underlined the important -- the relevant parts. This is about a comparative study done between Bosnian refugees. Again there was an expectation also for former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia. This is a comparative study between Bosnian refugees and Slovenian adolescents. In relation to suicide, this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to slow you down. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. And in this study, it says that it was precisely the Slovenian adolescents, that they were likely to more frequently express their desire to commit suicide when we compare this to their Bosnian refugees of the same age who had suffered war. Now, if we continue, as Mr. Turner expressed, his expectation that there would be an increase in the suicide rate, but he did not state the reference which would confirm this. It can happen that these expectations are not met, as it happened here in this study I gave as an example. So I am still trying to what we expect we give references for. The main problem with Dr. Turner's report is that things were not concrete enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you received the Rosner abstract? Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, do you have Rosner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Rosner is there, but I think no questions were allowed before we -- before the break or -- I'm listening to the witness and not reading Rosner at the same time. It was not a matter of putting it on our desk and then the way to Rosner was open. No, it was that the Prosecution would have an opportunity to read the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. Very well. Of course. Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's forget Rosner. What can you tell us, Doctor, about the figures which - let me check it - that you were also able to analyse concerning the problem of the -- I'm referring to -- by the authors of Begovic and others. What are the conclusions that you can draw from it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to mention this text because that is where we started yesterday, that is, the first group of the three articles, where I mentioned what Turner says in his report about 119 killed or wounded a day in Sarajevo, so that I could find Begovic's, Mazlagic's, and other's article, having to do with the state hospital, One of the two largest hospitals in Sarajevo, mentioned in the previous article. So now we are talking only about what exists in photocopies, and here he gives us 3.215 war injuries over a certain period of time. That is when one calculates, one when divides it by the number of days, we shall have 13 a day or 18. I cannot say precisely. I know that it's 13 for one and 18 for the other, but I do not think it is all that relevant because I will immediately now move on to mention another article, and this author is Drnda, it's the next one after which I've mentioned who says "40 months of Sarajevo." And when one calculates how many injured were admitted and we add those two figures up and so we get the figure of 31, which is at significant variance with the figure of 119. But I also have to mention that none of these three papers covers fully the period covered by General Galic's indictment, so that all this is an approximation, and it indicates a discrepancy between these figures and Turner's reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have two more questions, and then I will have finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about figures, and I'd like you to explain to us what are the relations that one can establish between the general -- the overall figure of persons who were victims of the war, that is, wounded and killed, during the period under consideration? Do you know these figures, at least approximately, and the idea, the notion of terror?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, I'd like to say what I objected to in the beginning, as to how we are to distinguish the war in Sarajevo and beyond Sarajevo. I told you yesterday that we had -- that we had to -- when we talked about the number of injuries on a war day in Sarajevo, and Mr. Turner spoke about -- said that that number was high and that that gives rise to fear and terror in all inhabitants of Sarajevo. And he also says that all inhabitants of Sarajevo, day in, day out, fight to survive. To my mind, this lacks precision, because all of us who are in this courtroom daily fight to survive. And the question is, what Dr. Turner said, whether this is applicable to all respondents, and I can tell you on the basis of my personal research how many people were injured and how they were injured, that those facts need not mean that they are suffering from such a severe mental trauma, that is, the mental trauma need not correspond to the bodily injury. According to my research, I concluded that the degree of their mental trauma depends on the -- on their subjective assessment of their injury, and if their subjective assessment -- although, their subjective assessment need not be realistic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question has already been answered in part, but I'd like -- and this is a difficult exercise; however, I'd like to ask you to sum up for us if possible in what way Dr. Turner's analysis was especially correct or especially incorrect or both -- for the Serb booth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Turner's analysis was not governed by the principles of systematical research, wasn't governed by the rules which lead us to a truthful conclusion. In other words, the sample was not adequate, it wasn't a random sample. Psychiatric instruments or interviews were not used. The witnesses during the hearing could be brought in a mental state which significantly changes, affects, the veracity of their statements. And so not even a verification scale was applied, that is, no control questions were used. The scale of socially correct, desirable answers, or truths and lies, as it had to do with the investigation of responsibility of a particular man for something. There was no analysis of factors which could have been significant for the evolution of terror and not what he stands accused of, because we know that fears are often learnt, and that is a known phenomenon in psychiatry, so that the media role was of -- the media role was significant, as well as all the preceding or following events or the events that followed the period for which General Galic stands accused of. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. All of this could have affected the subsequent cognitive processing of the information and affect the perception of the overall wartime situation, which would be different than it actually was. Likewise, I wanted here -- I am doing my best not to be biased but to shed more light on the subject, and I've also brought findings from literature which shed a different light on the period of Sarajevo, when -- that is, according to the reports, there was no purposeful starvation, when the courses were still held at the school of medicine. People studied, graduated, defended their doctoral thesis, experiments with animals were being conducted. And since I was also engaged in this, I know how demanding all this is, how expensive all that is, and how technical and difficult it is if you do not have adequate conditions. I also supplied an article which refers to CT scanners and which according that paper -- and we know how sensitive that equipment is, how it functioned with the same frequency during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Ready to start, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, your report is dated, I think, the 14th of January, 2003, and you say in it that you were engaged "to give my opinion on the report of Dr. Turner." When did you receive Dr. Turner's report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received Dr. Turner's report at a moment when I was engaged, and that was -- I cannot give you the date, but it was in December, I think. It was the former part of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: December of 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you read Dr. Turner's report, did you look at the references that he listed? I think it's the last two pages. Did you look at them and did you read them?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the references indicated. Some of the references, I was -- even I was familiar with some of these references, having learnt about them when I studied stress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is - yes or no - did you read them?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, yes, some of them, those which I had read previously, and yes, I was familiar with the author's names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether you read them before you were given this task or whether you read them after you were given this task, do you tell this Trial Chamber that you have read not just the abstracts but the various articles and other publications that Dr. Turner refers to in his report; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that I had read some articles. I don't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether there's any confusion, Mr. Ierace, but I did understand your answer to be that some of the references you had read already, and I took it then that you didn't read others. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you've understood me perfectly. I was familiar with some of them, but I did not search for the references indicated. I did not read them again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, I want to know whether at some stage in your life you have read each and every one of the articles and other publications that Dr. Turner referred to in his report. Could you answer that question with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about page 2, I see that I have the literary bibliography in Serb and the Oxford dictionary. If you want -- when one uses that, does that mean that one has to read all the Oxford dictionary? So that is a question. Could this be made more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question is quite clear. Mr. Ierace seems not to be satisfied with the answer, which is not in a direct yes or no. I think you said that you did not read all the references mentioned by Dr. Turner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you understood me well a moment ago. I don't know -- I don't see what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The answer has been given, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a few moments ago you gave some evidence in relation to some calculations that you did based on the abstracts. Would you please go to the abstract from the article by Mr. Drnda, I think it is pronounced. Now, firstly, this refers to the Centre for Emergency Medicine of the University Medical Centre in Sarajevo. Have you ever been to that centre?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether that centre is attached to Kosevo Hospital? Do you know whether it is independent -- it is independently located, that is, not in the Kosevo Hospital complex, or what?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put that question to the Defence, and they told me that it is related to the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now, could you explain to me how you arrived at the figure of 31. Firstly, what did you understand to be the relevant number of patients and what did you understand to be the figure of the relevant number of days? Perhaps you could give us those figures and explain where they appear in the abstract.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that when one adds up two papers, one gets 31. So I'm talking about the first paper, Drnda, which says 42.075 injured and sick. Of them 37 per cent were injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the next sentence, that is, two sentences further down, do these words appear, "In this period of time, 107.453 patients were treated hospitably with an average of 2.108 hospital beds. Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What period of time do you read the author of this abstract as referring to?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can do is read you the first sentence, in which he says, "Over 40 months."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, would you accept from me that -- well, first of all, do you accept that 40 days [sic] is the equivalent of 1.217 days? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you are referring to a month, Mr. Ierace, 40 months. You said "40 days."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: 40 months. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you accept that that is the equivalent of 40 months?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you give me a calculator, I'll be able to tell you exactly. But, say, 40 times 30 or 31, that would be the number of days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you can check this later if you like, during the next break, perhaps, but by my calculations when you divide the figure of 107.453 by the number 1.217, the result is 88.something. If that calculation is correct, does it appear from the abstract that over a 40-month period of the war, there was an average of 88 patients per day treated hospitably?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd merely like to remind you that this is the number of admitted which embraces both the injured and sick, and there are percentages referring to what are injuries, then what are acute, that is, surgery-requiring conditions, appendicitis or whatever, and that is a per cent of emergency cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The time, Dr. Kuljic. In question I asked you was in relation to the result of a mathematical Pages blanches insérées aux fins d’assurer la correspondance entre la pagination anglaise et la pagination française. calculation of 88 per day. Perhaps we'll leave it at that until you have a chance to check the maths. Let's now look at the point you raised and let's see if we can correlate the first sentence with the third. In the first sentence, is there a reference in relation to that figure of 42.075 to them being in the primary care unit and a reference also to the emergency department? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the third sentence, we see a reference to hospitalisation, as opposed to primary care or attendance at an emergency centre. I suggest to you that that is a possible explanation of why there are two different figures, noting, of course, that we don't have the full article. Do you agree that that is a possible explanation as to why there are two different figures in those two sentences?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd be happy if you allowed me to explain to you certain things, since I'm a physician, on the basis of common practice of admission into a hospital. So, patients come to the admission room, to the reception room, and that is this figure of 42.000. After that it is established how many injuries there were and after that they were admitted into different wards, except that we do not have this 107 [as interpreted] statistical breakdown into sick and injured, I mean with war injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Dr. Kuljic. You've told us you haven't been to this place. Your answer, I take it, is based on your experience in hospitals. Do you agree with me that it would be very helpful if you and I and others had this article, which is abstracted on this piece of paper, so that we could learn more about what these different figures represent? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my agreement with you or not should be tantamount to saying that we should all go to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please -- Dr. Kuljic, would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Instead of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't require further answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But would you refrain from commenting on what the consequences of your answer not yet given would be. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you offer yourself as an expert in this trial, don't you, an expert in relation to terror; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You come here offering an opinion as to the report of Dr. Turner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an expert, do you not think it appropriate to read the articles that you give evidence about before you get in the witness box?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But an abstract is also a part of an article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This article, according to the piece of paper we have, was published, it would seem, in a journal in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that the site from which you obtained this abstract is, I think it was suggested to you, a professional site, a site for professionals. When did you first discover this abstract on that site?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found this abstract after I submitted my report, because I continued working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Doctor, when? Not was it before or after you did your report, but when? Was it last week, last month?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, well, in January, say, the latter half of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've had time, if you wanted to, to read the report or the article in its full version; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was a large number of articles. Besides, to get this article, I would have to pay a certain, say, due or a tax. But this was accessible and this is what I used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was there any reason which prevented you from obtaining a copy? I appreciate you would have had to pay a fee, but I assume that's something you could have done. If you'd wanted to, could you have read the full article? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you that with us there is a problem with paying such fees and dues, since Internet articles, when you want to gain access to them, in extenso, then you have to pay it with your credit card. I don't have one, and a large number of people in Yugoslavia don't. It simply does not work in there, so that we are forced to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the first question is that this would be a convenient time. And -- But before having a break, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what did you want to bring to your attention?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. If this line of questioning is to continue, with regard to some personal -- I'd rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break anyhow. Is it something that would be proper to address in the presence of the witness that you would like to say, or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: To save time, Mr. President, I don't intend to pursue this line of questioning any further at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would that still make your intervention necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Just a comment. Every one of us should look at the end of the pointer when he intends to speak because we are otherwise all speaking -- because there is a cacophony there of different voices. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please escort the witness into the courtroom, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, I take it that you speak and read English, given that the abstracts are in the English language. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you read the English version of Dr. Turner's report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I read the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you check the English version of your report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do I take it that you are satisfied with the accuracy of the English version of your report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some minor observations. In one place, instead of "delusions," it was "madness" and some other things that would have changed the meaning significantly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make appropriate corrections to the English version of your report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that there are no errors that should be corrected, significant errors that should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the English version of your report, you refer sometimes to terror, sometimes to anxiety, sometimes to fear. What is the Serbian word for terror? And I'd like you, please, to spell it.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which word? Could you please repeat. Which word do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The word is "terror."

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is extreme fear, but in Serbian we frequently use the actual Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. word "terror."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the English word "terror"? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the word "terror," in many translations it is translated as "terror," although sometimes there could be some confusion with "fear."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to interrupt, but to the extent that the Prosecution wishes it, perhaps the word "Strah" S-t-r-a-h, should be transcribed. This is what the Prosecution wanted and spelled by the doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he -- I take it then that he did pronounce that word, because I cannot see that, of course, in the translation. You were asked, Dr. Kuljic, to give the Serbian term for what is called in English "terror," and from the transcript we only see that the word "terror" could be used as well. We were just informed that you also used the word "Strah." Is that correct? A Serbian word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be extreme fear. "Strah" is fear. But extreme fear is terror. It is in that sense. But the other meaning, for "terrorise," to terrorise someone, in some legal term, that's a different meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, suddenly I do not have the interpretation from the French booth. Perhaps because of the panel. Well, I was informed fully. I thank the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I did not have in my transcript the response of the French booth. Could you -- could the French booth repeat what I just said so that it will be translated in English and that Mr. -- that the Prosecution also can understand it. Perhaps I could solve it in a different way. I do understand that - but I just switched to the French channel - that the French interpreters explained to Mr. Piletta-Zanin that sometimes you need some reflection before you translate. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You should --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we cannot know that because we do not hear the French booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... At this moment, and I have -- yes. Thank you. So that is now clear, what was said. Yes. Then please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that terror was used in Serbian with either the English word "terror" or by using the words meaning "extreme fear." Was the Defence correct in saying that you used "Strah" to indicate extreme fear or not?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As extreme fear, extreme fear is not the same thing as ordinary fear. I think that is clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Spell, please, the Serbian words to convey extreme fear.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: E -- I'm spelling. E-k-s-t-r-e-m-n-i; second word, S-t-r-a-h.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that "strah" means fear. Does it also mean anxiety?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will now explain a little further, perhaps from the linguistics we could go on to psychiatry, which is why I was summoned here. So anxiety would include the state of tension --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. In your report, would you agree with me that by comparing the English word "anxiety" with the Serbian original, one can see that you sometimes translated "Strah" as "anxiety"? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you could show me specifically. Then I could explain on the basis of that. Could you give me a concrete example, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that when we go through your report. Do you agree with Dr. Turner's definition of "terror"?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The definition of "terror", as "extreme fear," as given by Dr. Turner, this will depend whether we are talking about the linguistic aspects of this meaning or psychiatric or legal aspects. And I would like here for us to discuss psychiatric aspects of fear, its extreme form --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness have his microphones adjusted, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The interpreter's booth asks that the witness's microphone be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that here we have a very clear example where the witness has to be authorised to respond, to respond in his domain. He was going to give an answer, and he was interrupted by the Prosecution. We think that this should not be accepted. Thank you. I'm referring to the transcript, Mr. President, line 13 of the current page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just reading it. The question was whether you agree with Dr. Turner's definitions of "terror," and you said it depends on whether you're talking about linguistic aspects or the meaning of this meaning or the psychiatric or legal aspects. You may explain to the Chamber whether you agree with the definition of "terror" in the psychiatric sense of this term, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you hear me on that before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have done so, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The relevant part of Dr. Turner's report is paragraph 4. I'll read the sentence: "The Concise Oxford Dictionary, 1976, gives a number of definitions for "terror" but the first and simplest is "a state of extreme fear." That's the definition given by Dr. Turner. I haven't asked the witness for a psychiatric definition, a medical definition, but I've drawn his attention to that as the simplest definition of "terror."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course you may ask the witness to express himself on the -- I would say the ordinary meaning of what a dictionary says, which is the simplest way of understanding this term. But if the witness could like to explain whether he agrees with psychiatric -- you just want to concentrate on this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's -- that's why I cut the witness short. And at that point before I could rephrase it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It -- yes. Please first answer the question of Mr. Ierace, as we understand it now to be, that is, the understanding of "terror" as a state of extreme fear, whether you would agree with that part of the report of Dr. Turner, as being the simplest definition of "terror."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is indeed a very brief definition of "terror," but it's rather simplified, particularly after that we can have a look at the meaning what is a terrorist. So the extreme fear does not have to be felt only in the cases that are later -- which is later defined in the definition of terrorism -- of a terrorist, so this is a very important question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The terrorist issue is not the issue Mr. Ierace wants to raise. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace. If you would need, at any further stage, for a better understanding of your testimony, that you would consider it of importance to explain your psychiatric view on that, you'll be given an opportunity to do that. But at this moment, would you please answer the questions of Mr. Ierace, which are just limited to the definition mentioned by Dr. Turner. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report at paragraph 2.1, you purported to repeat --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At paragraph 2.1, you purported to repeat the instructions given to Dr. Turner, and in so doing, I take it, you set out what you understood to be the objective of his report; is that correct? Is that what you understood to be the objective of his report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am just rereading it once again, just so that there is no confusion, just like I waited for you to read the abstracts and I didn't rush you, so I'm just asking you to -- not to rush me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have such a request to one of the parties, would you please address me so that I can -- if you have any problem with the way you're examined, please address me. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's what you understood to be his objective; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, I'd like to apologise to the President, and then I would like to answer. Yes, that is correct. That is how I understood. That's what was written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you checked the English version of your report. I'd like to suggest to you that you have misstated his instructions and in so doing misstated the objective of his report. Firstly, I will read to you from Dr. Turner's report in English what he said. And as I read it, please follow your words in your report. On paragraph 3 of Dr. Turner's report, last sentence, and the last sentence follows an outline of the essence of the charges against General Galic. "I have been instructed to prepare a report dealing with the relationship between events of this type and the production of terror." I suggest to you that those words do not appear in their entirety in your restatement of Dr. Turner's instructions. Instead we read: "I was given instructions to prepare an expert --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do not answer yet the question. Could you finish the question, unless the objection would be such that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object because now one is based on something which is a translation of a document which was written in Serbian, where one reads the text in Serbian, and that is the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is a comment to the question, as a matter of fact, and part of a possible answer. It is a matter that might be quite understandable to come up in your mind, but it's not an issue, it's not an objection against the question. So it's denied. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness was asked specifically by me whether he had checked the English version of his report, which makes the intervention doubly inappropriate. I'd be grateful if the time taken by interventions would not be detracted from my period. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll reread the words which appear in your report: "I was given instructions to prepare an expert opinion on the manner in which such events are influencing a creation of anxiety." I suggest to you there are two differences between what Dr. Turner has written and what you wrote. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd first like to say that I was unable to follow you. It was too fast for me. And that after that I managed to look at Dr. Turner's introduction, that is, his translation into Serbian and my version in Serbian, and they fully overlap. Now, tell me which versions should I compare? Which Serbian version and which English version?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have with you an English version of Dr. Turner's report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask for one?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think it necessary because it was a certified translation into Serbian. What would have happened had I not -- if I didn't know any English? And that is why I accepted this version in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So is it fair to say, is it accurate to say that you have at least until this minute always been under the apprehension, you have always understood that Dr. Turner --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to say something, in the absence of the witness. I'd like to say something in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Dr. Kuljic for one moment out of the courtroom. I have to ask you to leave for a second, Dr. Kuljic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I was looking in your direction and -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no possible error. Mr. President, what I wanted to say is the following: I have in front of me the translation of Mr. Turner's report done by the Prosecution's service itself, and its number is ERN 03054237. I've checked, and Dr. Turner quotes very exactly, as of page 2, to the -- at the end of page 2 to the beginning of page 3 the passage which is in inverted commas, in inversions, on page 2 -- I'm not going to read it in Serb. I can do it if necessary. But the word used is exactly this word, "Strah" which the Prosecution objects to. So if the Prosecution did this translation and if the expert based his opinion on that, then the witness cannot be reproached for that, for taking literally a document which was supplied by the Prosecution. So that is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are commenting both on what the Prosecution does and intends to do. And what became clear from the testimony of the witness is that he said that he copied the Serbian language as it appears in the translation in his own report that subsequently was translated in English as well. So, therefore, I -- what Mr. Ierace then did is, I would -- at least how I understood that Mr. Ierace was proceeding, that he wanted to verify that because of perhaps a bad translation, perhaps a good translation - I do not know - I do not know whether Mr. Ierace objected against "Strah" or not. I didn't hear him say -- I didn't hear him object. He was just trying to find out what words were used. But then he tried to find out whether the expert witness might have had a wrong opinion, whoever were to be blamed for that, but a wrong understanding of what the report of Dr. Turner was about. This is how I understood that. And I do not understand what -- why it is at this moment necessary, it becomes first of all quite clear from the testimony the way the expert witness proceeded in preparing his report. And you introduced a few things that are, as far as I understood the position of the Prosecution, were not said nor intended. So I think we could have just continued without this intervention but -- yes. But Judge Nieto-Navia would have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I will request to Mr. Piletta-Zanin to read the Serbian translation of Turner's report, the sentence. And I will ask the -- I will ask the interpreters not to translate that. The second time -- you should read that twice, please. The second time you can interpret that. Just to check -- I am checking, page 2 of the Serb original report of Mr. Kuljic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should be happy to do that, but I apologise to everybody for my pronunciation of Serbian. But I'm happy to do that it. I understand first you want me to read first point 2.1, which Mr. Kuljic quotes. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: No, no. I would like you -- Mr. Kuljic is quoting something from Turner's report. I would like you to read, or Ms. Pilipovic if you want, the quoted sentence in the Turner's translation in Serb. That's what I would like. I have here page 2 of the Serbian report. What I would like is to check that. I don't speak Serb, of course. So if you read slowly, I can follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should be happy to do that.
