And I quote, Mr. President, the last sentence of item 3 of the Turner report translated into the Serbian by the Prosecution, 03054237 is its ERN number, and 38. Now I'm quoting in Serbian. And we shall not have the interpretation of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [B/C/S spoken], [In English] End of quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes. Now we can get the interpretation if you read that again, just for the transcript, because -- of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should be happy to do that. So that same quotation, the same place: "I received the instructions so to prepare an expert opinion on how such events affected the production of fear." I apologise for my accent, but that is how it was translated, end of quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just while he's coming in, Mr. President, for the record Mr. Piletta-Zanin has twice said that it was the Prosecution's translation. I think he well knows it's CLSS that does the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, up until now, at least, has it been your understanding that the objective of Dr. Turner's report was to prepare an opinion on how such events affected the production of fear or anxiety?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I have written it, on how they affected, whether they resulted in the production of fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you read the transcript of the evidence of Dr. Turner?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you read that evidence, did it not become clear to you and indeed as you read the other parts of Dr. Turner's report, did it not become clear to you that he was concerned with terror rather than fear or anxiety?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't ask me when is it that I read the transcript. I did that after I'd written my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's irrelevant for my question, Dr. Kuljic. If you could please respond to my question. Do you want me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Repeat it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you read the transcript of Dr. Turner's evidence and the other parts of Dr. Turner's report, did it not become clear to you that Dr. Turner in his report was concerned with terror rather than fear or anxiety?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His interest in his report lay with how -- what are the origins of fear, what are the mechanisms leading to fear. And at the end of the report it is said that the objective -- that the reasons behind all these objectives was to produce terror, to cause terror. That is what I thought having read his report and having read the transcript later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have with you a copy of Dr. Turner's report in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please turn to paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please read slowly out aloud the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Because of that, charges were laid against him which, among other things, charged him with unlawful terrorisation of civilians."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You can stop there.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Punishable by article -- under article --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Would you now please read the next heading, that is the heading above paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Definition of terror."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think the first sentence under that heading is the definition of "terror" according to a particular English dictionary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. In the dictionary several definitions, and the first definition is quoted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, no one would be critical of you for basing your understanding of Dr. Turner's report on the Serbian interpretation you were given, but did it not seem odd to you that the charge against General Galic, which was relevant to the report, dealt with terrorisation and Dr. Turner in his report dealt with terror? Did that not seem odd to you, therefore, that he expressed his instructions to be -- to prepare a report involving fear or anxiety rather than terror?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain how did I understand this. So I understood that there was an indictment against General Galic, accusing him of conducting shelling and sniping campaign against civilian areas, and I won't go on reading it, and that the indictment charges him under Article 51 and so on. Then the next sentence said that an expert opinion should be prepared as to how such events, that is, events which seem to be considered as under his responsibility, how -- what is the role of such events in the production of fear. Then reading -- when one reads the report further, Dr. Turner often says that his findings are based on what he knows, and if that is accepted as correct in court. In other words, my understanding was that he wanted to say what degree of fear it was and to say how it all affected the behaviour of people exposed to it. And after that it will be possible to make a decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In -- would you please look at paragraph 2.2 of your report. Having stated, indeed having repeated verbatim Dr. Turner's instructions according to the Serbian translation of his report, you immediately observed what appeared to you to be an inconsistency between his stated objective at the beginning of his report and the terms of his conclusion at the end of his report. Have I correctly paraphrased or summarised what you say in paragraph 2.2?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is here, under 2.2, that I quoted directly what is written, since after that I concluded that this was the difference between these strict instructions, because my analysis on what could be the objective did not agree with what was a strict instruction, and the instruction was to present an opinion as to how -- what role these events play in the production of fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Now, earlier I suggested to you that there were two differences between the critical sentence of Dr. Turner, in which he set out his instructions, between the English version as it transpires and the Serbian version, as it appears in your report. I would now like to take you to a second difference. Firstly, for the sake of completeness, given that you read English, I would like you to look at the English version of Dr. Turner's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might the witness be shown that exhibit, which is, I think -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a long line that you would like to read, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It's P3716. It isn't, Mr. President. Perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Locate -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, if Mr. Ierace reads one or a few lines of the report, could you please follow on your screen the English text read and take your time to read it. Then we don't need the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So would you please first listen to Mr. Ierace and then take your time to read on the screen what he said, English version. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, as you might expect, the original of Dr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, and I think my objection is necessary for the possible future for the re-examination. I'd like to know what is in this document, because I do not have it in my memory. I think it is necessary to have it. Perhaps there will be some other things there which will be then quoted by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. You know the report. You'll see the relevant text on the screen. I take it that you prepared for the examination of this witness, which deals with the report of Dr. Turner, so that you are able to establish the context in which it was written. And of course in re-examination you could ask questions about it. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The original version of that sentence, Dr. Kuljic, which was in the English language, is as follows, and I quote: "I have been instructed to prepare a report dealing with the relationship between events of this type and the production of terror." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, take your time to read these two lines. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the first difference which we have just --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Kuljic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'd like -- I'd like to be given time to read it and then compare it with what it says in the report, if I may. After that, further questions may be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may take your time to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we have dealt with one of the differences between that sentence and its translation, namely the word "terror" appeared in the original but the Serbian version communicates instead the notion of fear or anxiety but not terror. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a difference between fear, "Strah", and terror, "teror."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I would like to draw to your attention what I suggest is a second critical difference, and that is whereas Dr. Turner's original sentence states as part of his objective to deal with the relationship between the events set out in the indictment and the production of terror, your -- the translation provided to you went a step further and refined the nature of the relationship to being a causal relationship between events of the type set out in the indictment and the creation of a particular state of mind. Firstly, do you understand my question or at least what I'm putting to you is a difference between the two statements?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now trying to repeat it so as to provide you with an answer to a second question. I'm still looking for a sentence which seems to have disappeared from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would need it, I will read it again to you. But the question is whether -- where the original report -- the original version deals with the relationship between events of this type and the production of terror. Mr. Ierace puts it to you that in the version on the basis of which you worked, mention is made of a causal relationship.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now I've got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you appreciate that there is that difference between the English original sentence and -- on the one hand, and the Serbian translation that you were given, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some differences; however, it is an issue of language and these language issues could make a difference in translation, in terms of some nuances of the language. Although, I would like us to discuss the Serbian version, my Serbian version and the Serbian version of the translation. That would make it a lot easier for me. And other issues can be discussed with translators. Otherwise, I need some specific questions that are to do with my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, please understand that I'm not being critical of you, firstly; and secondly, I pursue this matter for this reason, that ultimately I will be suggesting to you that your report and the report of Dr. Turner are at cross-purposes, if that could be translated. But we will do it step by step. Would you please now go to paragraph 3.1 of your report. Do you have that paragraph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point in your report you formulate a methodological question based on your understanding of Dr. Turner's objective, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, given your understanding that Dr. Turner was required to give an opinion as to how the events in Sarajevo alleged by the Prosecution affected the production of terror, you say that what Dr. Turner should have done was establish this question: "How can one respond to the request for evaluating the state of anxiety in Sarajevo in the period from 10 September 1992 to 10 August 1994?" I'm suggesting to you that is the relationship between your understanding of Dr. Turner's objective and the question you posed to yourself and the reader at paragraph 3.1. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this, I disagree with you because "terror," if we accept Dr. Turner's definition, is a state of extreme fear, which means that fear as such also includes extreme fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The English version of your report, no doubt you noted when you checked it, states -- refers to the state being evaluated as the state of anxiety. It does not say "the state of fear." It does not say "the state of extreme fear" or "state of terror." I suggest to you, therefore, that the task you set yourself as the appropriate task was to evaluate the state of anxiety in Sarajevo and that that is understandable given your understanding of Dr. Turner's objective.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to have some time to have a look at the translation into English so that I can find the sentence regarding what's been implied as being the problem with the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you could help me and tell me which page this is on so that we can save some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.1. If you do it by paragraphs, it might be faster.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I was thinking that you could give me a page number. That would be even easier. Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In the Serbian version, it is on page 4.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same page 4 in both Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think the word you use is "straha." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Here the word "fear," "strah" is mentioned and in the English version that's anxiety. So I'd like to explain the different between these two words, psychiatrically speaking. May I do that? Because I'm waiting for the authorisation to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you please -- is the issue that you say the English text reads "anxiety" where the witness has testified that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. terror is extreme fear? Is that the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It's whether -- whether it is translated into English as "fear" or "anxiety," there's still a -- a failure to connect, for lack of a better phrase, between -- going on the report the understanding of the writer compared to the contents of Dr. Turner's report. So it's not just linguistic. Perhaps I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said that you would like to explain something to us. What exactly would you like to explain? So before doing it, tell us what you would like to explain. The relation bet between anxiety and terror, or -- what would you like explain to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wish to explain is anxiety, fear, and terror, what we're talking about here. First of all, anxiety can be --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's not the issue. That's not the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the issue Mr. Ierace wants to raise at this very moment. So if at a later stage the Prosecution or the Defence would like to raise this issue, you'll certainly get an opportunity to explain. If you find it that vital for your opinion, you always can ask at the end of your testimony whether you can explain that. Please Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Just for the transcript, I can see that on page -- line 22 of the previous page and the following, let us say until page 56, the Prosecution explained very clearly what they wanted. And I think this is a way of saying things in front of the witness that should have been stated in his absence. I'm stating this for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is in the record. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, from that point onwards, your report, not entirely but in a large part, is devoted to the proposition of a study which would achieve the, or respond to the methodological question that you set yourself at paragraph 3.1. Would you agree with that? It sets the direction for your report.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I said was that what has to be examined was the state of fear and events that caused it, and for both things there are certain psychiatric instruments, also for the events that occurred that caused the fear or its extreme variant, that is, terror. So their existence and also the existence of psychological, mental perception of it as such, more or less extensively, to a higher or lesser degree. So this is a complex issue which goes from -- not from A causing B but apart from that, many other factors can cause it on which I have extensively written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while you did that, Dr. Turner did something very different. Dr. Turner in his report evaluated the literature in relation to terror, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain places he quoted literature. In some places he quoted transcript from the trial proceedings, what the witnesses said, that is, witness testimony. And it is on the basis of that that he drew his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The structure of Dr. Turner's report, I suggest to you, is important to understand, and I suggest to you that that structure is an examination of the literature that exists in respect of terror and a comparison of how the characteristics of different aspects of terror match or don't match aspects of the evidence. Would you agree with me that is the structure of Dr. Turner's report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment, because I have a lot of paper here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you prefer I gave you some examples? Would that make it easier?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for that. I just want to have a look at it again so that I can answer your question. Here. Now, may I just direct you to item 3 of Dr. Turner's report, where under 3 he gives all the effects and also the instruction on how to prepare findings on how these factors influence production of fear. Now, my observation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a minute.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said item 3. I don't recognise the contents as you described them at either paragraph 3 or page 3. Can you be -- can you check whether it is item 3 of Dr. Turner's report.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Dr. Turner's report. It says "Introduction," and then after that it says item 3 or paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you read the first few words, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I was told that Stanislav Galic as the commander of --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Dr. Kuljic, the heading I took you to earlier of "Definition of terror" refers to a simple definition as being a state of extreme fear. Do you see that in your Serbian copy of his report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go to paragraph 11. At that paragraph do we see a subheading "Extreme fear"?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me read it. Paragraph 11, "Extreme fear," yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And thereafter, he refers to the literature as to the components of, firstly, fear. And then at paragraph -- different types of fear, and then at paragraph 14, he refers to factors relevant to the production of a persisting fear response. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I just need to find that page because it seems to have dropped out. Yes, I've found the page. So we've come to this. You said it was item 13. I'm sorry, can you repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 14, where he discusses Rachman. He seeks out the factors relevant to the production of a persisting fear response, four factors. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. I can see what's been given here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as he goes through those factors, he finds resonance in passages of transcript of evidence given in this trial, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as part of Rachman, as part of that, yes. But there is another question though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. You refer to these passages of transcript as samples, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, considering that the indictment is about the whole of Sarajevo. The way I see this is a kind of sample of people from Sarajevo and their testimonies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that as samples they fail basic tests. For instance, they are not representative samples, they do not allow for possible bias of those who come to this court to give their evidence, and so on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I state this because the indictment is for the whole of Sarajevo, and of course for the methodological errors that you have just raised, and I still stand by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Dr. Kuljic, I come now to the divergence, if I could put it that way, between your approach and that of Dr. Turner. By seeing these passages as poor samples, you are considering his task in terms of a different objective, an assessment or analysis of the state of anxiety generally in Sarajevo and a particular view to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object in relation to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't listen to you in French, and I -- I object in relation to ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object in relation to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't understand the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are not understood. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise. I wanted to be brief so that the witness wouldn't understand me. What I meant was sense, meaning. I meant semantic meaning. So one has to know in which language the witness spoke so that we know what was the meaning, what was the translation, so that we know what the witness meant. So it was on the level of seme, "s-e-m-e" that my objection was. Specifically on the level of seme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has a problem, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We do not understand your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it will save time, I'll withdraw the question and rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Turner never suggested that these passages represented representative samples of the population of Sarajevo, did he?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not mention that this was a representative sample, so I presume that he was aware of the limits that I stressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, I'm suggesting to you that you're criticising him for not doing something he never set out to do.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that on the basis of what was quoted here, these four points, among which there is a factor of personality, when Dr. Turner quotes a proverb, each person has a breaking point. However, this cannot be taken as something that is relevant for giving a scientific opinion, and there are many papers that say that certain people do not develop psychopathology that will bring them to the breaking point, not even in extreme situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that, but it's not responsive to what I'm putting to you. You're going to a particular comment made by Dr. Turner on that page. See, what I'm suggesting to you is that Dr. Turner's primary objective was to consider the professional literature, the literature in psychiatry and psychology in relation to terror, its characteristics, its causes, and then to look at aspects of the trial evidence to see if it was consistent or inconsistent. Having regard to the English version of Dr. Turner's objective, do you at least concede that that's what he did?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My objection is precisely about the way that he did it, the method, and that's why I said that such a report was not acceptable. Something that could be called a selective abstraction. When we are talking about Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. Please try to understand the comparison I make. What Mr. Ierace wants you to consider is in a comparison of the following: He says that an expert gives an expert opinion on what a car, on what an automobile is - that is usually four wheels, steering wheel, brakes, engine - and then he gives a few pictures, one of a Renault, one of a Zastava, another of a Plymouth. And then another expert comes and says on the basis of this report you could never establish how many cars are driving on the roads in Paris, one being a description of what the main characteristics are, according to literature, and the other expert concentrating on the distribution of cars in urban traffic. That is as a matter of fact, as far as I understand, the question that has been put to you, whether Dr. Turner is not aiming at establishing whether a state of terror existed in general terms in Sarajevo at that time, which perhaps would require samples and a study you think would be needed in order to establish such a thing and that therefore your report and Dr. Turner's report are dealing with different questions, although there is a similarity and that is that they both deal with, whether it's fear or terror or anxiety. Did I understand your questions to go in that direction? Could you please try to answer whether you would agree or would not agree that you're dealing with a different question as Dr. Turner did, and please try to keep in mind the comparison I made, which reflects more or less the difference suggested to you by Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After this explanation, I can say that apart from the distribution that you spoke about -- I'm not asking about how many cars there are in Paris. That could be one thing, one issue. But within that my comment is that if the car has four wheels, a door, and windows, we have to know that in order for the car to drive, it needs an engine. That is why I'm talking about other things that were not taken into consideration by Dr. Turner. That's one side of that. We can also look at my report in this way, that one part will speak about this distribution, as you mentioned, but another part of it will more closely look into cars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. But I think what Mr. Ierace did put to you is that to some extent, that if you want to know how many cars there are, you have to count them. If you just want to describe the car, you don't need to count them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to count them, but we're speaking about cars. We cannot not mention the engine. We have to mention the engine. But if you wish, we can leave it just like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's time for a break. We will adjourn until ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just while he's being brought in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin has requested an English copy of Dr. Turner's report. My case manager is obtaining one. And when she arrives, perhaps it could be passed to the usher so that he can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And I must have already submitted to the Prosecution the Serb version of the dictionary which gives the definition of terror. Once again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, I would like to move now to a different area. We've referred to the nature of the charges against General Galic, and I'm now talking about the terror charge, the charges which relate to the sniping and shelling of civilians deliberately in N what we might call the indictment period, that is, between the 10th of September, 1992 and the 10th of August, 1994. Would you agree that we can accept as a matter of ordinary human understanding that if a person is repeatedly targeted with a rifle or by shelling, that that will induce in them the state of extreme fear that we call terror?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like you to make your question more specific. Do you mean to say that all the inhabitants of Sarajevo were constantly targeted? So is that the question, whether all the inhabitants of Sarajevo were being aimed at and targeted by snipers all the time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me break my question into 1992 separate questions. The first question is: Would you agree that we can accept as a matter of ordinary human understanding that if a person is repeatedly targeted with a rifle or by shelling, that experience will induce in them the state of extreme fear that we call terror?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that fear one experiences in a particular situation depends precisely on how that person sees his or her situation, and that is a key point there. So if an individual sees it as a permanent danger, there will be fear. But as time passes by and that individual realise that is he/she is alive and is alive day after day, the fear decreases, because that person understands that he has survived through something that in the beginning was intense fear, so that I cannot give you a spatial answer. I have to do it on the basis of a temporal section of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, my question, I suggest to you, was a simple one, and I did not factor into it how that person might respond day after day or week after week. Can I at least have from you your acceptance that the experience of being targeted, being shot at deliberately, will in a person with a normal degree of robustness of mind nevertheless cause the sensation of terror rather than fear?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question, you said a person with a normal degree of robustness of mind, if I got your meaning correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Well, this is precisely one of the things. As you asked me that question, it is simplification, because we cannot talk about normal or abnormal person and how he or she experiences fear because it covers a whole range of degrees and emotions. But if your question is about an individual who is exposed for the first time in his or her life to targeting and thinks that he/she might be hit, that individual experiences intense fear, but its intensity decreases if that individual is aimed at every day but is not fired at. There is an adage which says don't ever threaten with an empty pistol, and I think that is a reference to Dr. Turner's words in his report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, you refer to the disorder known as the post-traumatic stress disorder. Would you agree with me that its usefulness in relation to this topic of terror is restricted because that disorder refers to a continuing prevalence of fear in individuals who suffer from it which lasts long after the traumatic event which caused it has passed?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just read your question once again, because it sounded rather long-winded, so let me -- So if I understand what you mean, you are asking me about the relationship between the experience of fear or terror and the post-traumatic stress disorder. So my answer would be that a person experiences that kind of fear, a certain percentage of people will suffer such a disorder but it varies from one individual to another over a period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many people exposed to the same trauma as that which causes that disorder in some individuals do not develop that disorder - do you agree with that - even though both might be of an otherwise robust state of mind?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right there. That is, two persons may be exposed to a particular event. One will develop such a disorder and the other one won't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To construct an example: If we have, say, a child who is repeatedly shot at and manages to -- or, say, two children who are repeatedly shot at and manage to survive the traumatic experience, one develops that disorder and the other does not. The fact that one develops it and the other does not does not detract from the fact that both experienced terror. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I got your meaning correctly, you mean that they can normally experience an identical situation and one develops such a disorder and the other doesn't. But it is another matter whether one child experiences that situation with intense fear and the other not. It also depends on whether after that the parents of a child keep repeating, "Yes, you could have got killed, you could have died," and the parents of the other child say, "Well, it's okay, it's over." So it can also depend whether an individual will be additionally traumatised and suffer from this disorder or not. I keep saying that it depends very much on one's -- on one individual's perception of the trauma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, in your answer you focussed on whether one child might have experienced terror, whereas the other did not. In my hypothetical example, accept that both children experienced terror but one develops the disorder and the other does not, firstly, is that a scenario which could occur where both children are of a robust state of mind?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means, this thing that you asked me now, is whether those children perceive the trauma in an identical way. Perhaps they did not. Perhaps one perceived it as more dangerous and the other one perceived it as less dangerous. And after that this other thing comes that you asked about, the issue of robustness of mind, who will develop -- so it is one's perception of something, whether we perceive something as dangerous. So let us divide it into parts. It is after that that you start thinking about it. So if somebody did not notice anything, he will not start a fear. If he did, then it is his or her robustness will determine whether the disorder will develop or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, you are required for the purposes of that question to accept the hypothetical basis, and you have not done that. Let me try it a different way. If a study reveals that, let's say, 50 per cent of a population following an event, a traumatic event, experienced by that population, have the disorder, the post-traumatic stress disorder, that does not mean necessarily, does it, that only 50 per cent of them experienced the sensation of terror at the time of the traumatic event, does it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True, it does not need to mean that, and I mentioned a moment ago that it doesn't mean that not -- that does not mean that not everybody was afraid. That is what I already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, a further difficulty with relying on rates of post-traumatic stress disorder is that, with the passing of time, many sufferers of that disorder recover, don't they?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the time passing by after a trauma, in case post-traumatic stress disorder has taken place, there are two possibilities, at least two possibilities: One is that a person is still exposed to something, for instance, has a traffic accident, and then acquires the post-traumatic stress disorder and constantly has on his mind the picture of the smashed car, and every time he sees that picture that person is traumatised over and over again, which then will exacerbate symptoms and therein the role of the media and subsequent cognitive processing of any traumatic experience. And on the other hand, there are numerous papers speaking about the aggravation of symptoms in holocaust victims --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please read my question on the screen. And if you like, I'll repeat it. What I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it. Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- and the answer is that a certain number of people will see the reduction in the number of symptoms and in others that will not be the case. I've just explained it to you, when the symptoms persevere, and we have Dutch [as interpreted] psychiatrists who study people who 30 years on have still had a high degree of psych disorders and PTSD, just as it happens in situations I have mentioned, for instance, this example with the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Putting it simply, many people who have that disorder recover over time, don't they?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say a certain percentage. I wouldn't say many people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many studies have been done as to the percentage of people who retain the condition for the rest of their life, haven't there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. To give one example, Dr. Turner in his report speaks or has written about the experience of rape, how although that is a very powerful experience in terms of trauma, over time the recovery rate from post-traumatic stress disorder is quite good. Do you remember reading that in his report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is an annex. There is a table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Now, in your report -- would you please go to paragraph 5.3 and in particular the last sentence of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said 5 ...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you refer there to a particular study, and according to the study almost every man who had a war experience was developing a PTSD. You obviously thought that important to put in the report. Why? What is the relevance of that observation from that report? How does it contribute to your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This comment had to do with the sex, and this was done by Chester and associates. This was a study conducted with American Indians, and it was to show the difference in the way that traumas are experienced and exposure to trauma. There is another item where I speak about the exposure rate and evolution of traumas. And this is a fact which has to do with those respondents. As I have said, every author always makes a reservation and says that he's dealing with a particular population because there are other papers which indicate different rates, and I also mentioned that in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, would you look at my question. What is the relevance of that observation? How does it contribute to your conclusions? You've mentioned it has to do with the sex. Is there any other relevance in that sentence, that is, other than sex?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I was writing this, I had in mind the last sentence, that these differences show that it is indispensable to bear in mind the sex structure of the population under consideration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, could you tell us, what does it matter, if sex is the point, as to what the traumatic event was that caused the disorder? Why do you mention that almost every man who had a war experience was developing that disorder? Why don't you just point out what the percentage of men was with the disorder compared to the percentage of women?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mentioned, is that almost every man with a war experience developed the PTSD, addresses only that paper. It was up to me to clarify the difference between men and women. So that was the gist of it, not the to emphasise something else, that every man reacted like this. There are also cultural differences regarding the perception of trauma in every society. I could also quote to you some of the researches done in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I ask you how much time you'd still need. We're coming close to two hours, even if we deduct many moments, especially the moments where the witness had to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at least 20 minutes and beyond. The Defence took much longer than the time they were allocated. There have been fresh matters. In fact, I've just now, while I've been on my feet, received some copies of the relevant materials which I'll need to read overnight. But perhaps I could review it overnight, Mr. President, after I finish tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber compared the times taken by the Defence and by the Prosecution. You may proceed if there's -- we'll indicate at the end of this hearing how much time would still be available, but you can continue until 7.00. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we are speaking of time passing. I don't know what is the position of your Chamber in relation to the Rosner papers. I think it's Rosner papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would there be any objection, Mr. Ierace, from the side of the Prosecution having in mind the abstract given of the article of Dr. Rosner that questions would be put to the witness in respect of that abstract?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, my position remains the same: That when we're dealing with expert psychiatrists on such a critical issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- The least we could expect are copies of the full articles. And at this stage we have an extract which has been provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow questions on the Rosner abstract, but could you please keep in mind that it is an abstract, which of course could create some problems. And you took already far more time than granted, so it is not a subject for extensive questioning, but a few questions will be allowed. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that paper with you, the copy that you read?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paper do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the paper by Robin and Chester that you refer to in your report.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that you come to give evidence and don't bring with you the reports that you quote or summarise passages from in your report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I took with me all the papers, then I would have to bring all of my literature from psychiatry and on stress, so I would need a lot of time to gather that in my home in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. How big was the sample of men in that study, just approximately?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall now exactly what the sample was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you exactly. I'm asking approximately.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was not a large study, an extensive study with a large number of persons questioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, would you disagree with me if I told you that in fact ten men had a war experience in that study? Does that accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would correspond to what I said, that it was not an extensive study.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would not surely have been wise to repeat in this report a conclusion as to the percentage of men who had a war experience who went on to develop this disorder where the sample, where the group, was only ten, I suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that as one of the references, not as a key reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the report also made clear that the study was on a particularly troubled community in North America, troubled in the sense that its members had experienced a number of different traumatic events. Does that accord with your recollection of the article?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it not the case that it becomes difficult to discern which traumatic events, where a person has experienced a number, have contributed to the disorder?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a cumulative effect of events bearing on the symptoms of psychopathology, starting from the earliest childhood days from the moment when a key event occurs and following that, even events after that key event can influence and influence the appearance of symptoms of psychopathology which is what I stated in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In the interests of saving time, I think you would agree with the proposition that I put to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I ask you that many traumas can have cumulative effect? Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, specifically, that it can become difficult to discern which traumatic events, where a person has experienced a number, have contributed to the disorder. And I think you agree with that. Is that so? If you can answer with a yes or no, please do.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I can't answer. I have to explain psychiatric practice. Every time we ask a person which one was the key event --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I withdraw the question. And if you wish it, I have copies of this report. But does this conclusion ring a bell with you? Do you remember this conclusion from the report: "The high prevalence of PTSD in this community is therefore more likely due to a high rate of exposure to trauma and the types of traumatic events than to any specific vulnerability to PTSD." Do you remember reading the conclusion of the report?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the report in its entirely a while ago, which is why I cannot tell you about each one. But there is something which is key and sometimes we assess whether there was some that was less significant or some more significant causes that would have triggered this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Doctor, this was a community that had a lot of problems generating regular traumatic experiences, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please turn to paragraph 6.1 of your report, in particular the last two sentences. There you refer to Kessler and associates, and you state that in their report they make clear that the life prevalence in the general population of PTSD is 5 per cent for women and 10 per cent for men. Now, stopping there for the moment, first of all, what is the relevance of the percentage between the sexes in terms of terror in Sarajevo in the indictment period? Can you very briefly tell us, if you can in a sentence, what's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the terror in Sarajevo and any other, so let us assume that there are some differences between men and women and in each medical research it is always stressed how many women there were and how many men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we already know that the existence of the disorder is not a determinant of whether the individual experienced terror at the time of the traumatic event, don't we?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't have to be that a person had suffered this fear and did not develop the disorder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in any event, I suggest to you that you got the figures wrong. I suggest to you that the figures given by Kessler and associates in that report is the reverse, 10 per cent for women and 5 per cent for men. If you like, I can show you the report. But perhaps you remember.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to have a look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we'll leave that with you overnight. Now, you go on to say that in that report the authors quote the life prevalence for exposure to traumatic experience as 25 per cent for men and 13 per cent for women. Now, firstly, a word of explanation. Does life prevalence mean the percentage of persons who suffer the disorder who retain it for the duration of their life?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second part that you mentioned, for life prevalence for exposure to traumatic experiences, so that's how much people are exposed to traumatic experiences, not how many developed pathological -- psychopathological symptoms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that 25 per cent of men are exposed to traumatic experiences for the duration of their life. Is that your interpretation of "life prevalence"?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to their perception. We can now speculate in relation to this that everybody goes through traumatic experiences. We can speculate in this way. But this is in relation to what is accepted to be a traumatic experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, "life prevalence" is a phrase which occurs repeatedly in the literature in relation to this disorder, isn't it? It's a common indicator in the reports, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're saying that where we read that term, "life prevalence," what it means or what it refers to is the exposure to traumatic experience over a lifetime. Is that what you're saying, or have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Again I suggest to you that you got the figures wrong. I suggest to you - and you can read it overnight - that the figures are not 25 per cent for men but 60.7 per cent for men, and not 13 per cent for one but 51.2 per cent for women. If you're not able to answer that without first reading the report, please say so.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I have to look at the paper again. I have to read it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, perhaps we can just deal quickly with one other small issue. Today you referred to the extract of the study by Jensen. Do you remember that and do you have a copy with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to indicate to the interpreters. I will need one minute at the end of Mr. Ierace's intervention, but I wanted to say this now while the doctor was looking for his article. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you had underlined a passage of this abstract and you read out what it said. But in reading it out, according to the English transcript of your evidence, you attributed to the abstract a definite connection between war-trauma-induced stress disorders and increases in suicide. Do you see the sentence beginning with the word "complications"? I'll read from there: "Complications related to war-trauma-induced stress disorders may give rise to significant increases in" and then later "suicides." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember now, I think this is the sentence that I read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except according to the transcript or the translation, you said "are." Not possible but definite that they -- in other words, that they do contribute to it, it does happen. So my first question is: Do you accept that according to the abstract war-trauma-induced stress disorders, complications related to them, may, that is, not definitely, give rise to significant increases in suicides? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall I read "may give." Perhaps this is not entered into the transcript. But it says here and there's no reason for me to read it differently. I've underlined it. "May give." So there is a supposition, an assumption -- we always take an assumption as a starting point in every research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I was just informed that we have to stop in time. In fact, we should always, but I have a bad record on that. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you asked one minute for translation issues, those that have to be -- cannot be dealt with in another way, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Very briefly: For the English booth, page 28, line 9, certain things were not interpreted to do with coffee, but it doesn't matter. Page 58, line 23, French booth, there is a countermeaning. Your report is not his report. Then on page 74, for the French booth interpreter, there is no such a thing as very traumatic, and the same for the French booth interpreter for page 77, there is also a countermeaning, 5 per cent for the women, 10 per cent for the men. In fact, it is the other way around. And the rhythm was rather rapid. On page 70 from the page -- from the French booth was not able to interpret that. There was one other thing which wasn't noted is that I was intervening out of respect for interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I give a copy of those two articles to the court usher to pass to the witness for overnight reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Kuljic, you could read this overnight if there would be any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, tomorrow there will be 15 effective minutes of cross-examination available to you. We will adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom. And may I instruct you, Dr. Kuljic, not to speak with anyone about your testimony. Yes, I instructed you yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 7.04 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of March, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
